title: Southwell and the poem
short: By the Jesuit Robert Southwell (executed at Tyburn, 1595); printed posthumously in 'Saint Peters Complaint' (1602). Jonson admired it greatly.
body: Robert Southwell (1561-95), an English Jesuit, worked secretly as a priest in England from 1586, was arrested in 1592, tortured and hanged at Tyburn on 21 February 1595; he was canonised in 1970. His poems circulated in manuscript among Catholics and were printed after his death, 'The Burning Babe' first in the 1602 edition of 'Saint Peters Complaint'. Ben Jonson told William Drummond that if he had written 'The Burning Babe' he would have been content to destroy many of his own poems. 'Hoary' means white with frost.

sources.cite: Catalogue of English Literary Manuscripts (CELM), Robert Southwell (first printing of 'The Burning Babe' in Saint Peters Complaint, 1602)
James H. McDonald and Nancy Pollard Brown (eds), The Poems of Robert Southwell, S.J. (Oxford, 1967)
Ben Jonson, Conversations with William Drummond of Hawthornden (1619)

anchor: Which made my heart to glow
title: Metre and vision form
short: Fourteen-syllable couplets (fourteeners), printed as alternating 8- and 6-syllable lines; the poem narrates a vision.
body: The poem is in fourteeners, long lines of seven stresses rhymed in couplets, here broken into alternating lines of eight and six syllables (the common metre of hymns and ballads). The plain, almost ballad-like movement carries a dense chain of paradoxes. The narrative frame is that of a vision: the speaker stands in the snow, is surprised by sudden heat, sees, hears a speech and, when the vision vanishes, understands. The heat that makes the heart 'glow' anticipates the moral of the poem, that the Christ-child's love should kindle human hearts.

sources.cite: James H. McDonald and Nancy Pollard Brown (eds), The Poems of Robert Southwell, S.J. (Oxford, 1967)
A. B. Grosart (ed.), The Complete Poems of Robert Southwell (1872)

anchor: A pretty babe all burning bright
title: The burning babe
short: The Christ-child appears in the air on fire: compare the burning bush (Exodus 3:2) and 'our God is a consuming fire' (Hebrews 12:29).
body: The vision of a child burning but not consumed recalls the burning bush in which God appeared to Moses (Exodus 3:2), a traditional type of the Virgin's conception, and God as 'a consuming fire' (Hebrews 12:29; Deuteronomy 4:24). 'Pretty' meant fine or comely rather than merely charming. The fire is the fire of divine love, and the infant's suffering looks forward to the Passion. The image is deliberately startling.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Exodus 3:2
The Bible (KJV), Hebrews 12:29

anchor: Such floods of tears did shed
title: Tears and flames
short: The paradox of tears that should quench the flames but are bred by them: sacred adaptation of Petrarchan fire-and-water conceits.
body: The child weeps floods of tears, as though they could quench his flames, yet the tears are themselves produced by the heat. Fire and water, burning and weeping, were the stock oxymorons of Petrarchan love poetry ('I burn and freeze'). Southwell deliberately converted secular love conventions to sacred subjects, as he says in the prefatory letter to his poems, and here the lover's sighs and tears become Christ's. 'Excessive' carries its root sense, going beyond measure.

sources.cite: James H. McDonald and Nancy Pollard Brown (eds), The Poems of Robert Southwell, S.J. (Oxford, 1967)
A. B. Grosart (ed.), The Complete Poems of Robert Southwell (1872)

title: fry
short: 'Fry' meant to burn or be consumed with heat, without the culinary sense dominating.
body: In the sixteenth century 'fry' could mean simply to burn, to be scorched or to suffer intense heat, of passion as well as of fire (OED 'fry', v.). The newborn Christ declares that he burns from the moment of his birth, so that the Nativity already contains the Passion. The verb is thus intense rather than comic, and the paradox of a newborn suffering in fire prepares for the furnace allegory that follows. The present tense makes the suffering immediate.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary
James H. McDonald and Nancy Pollard Brown (eds), The Poems of Robert Southwell, S.J. (Oxford, 1967)

anchor: none approach to warm their hearts
title: None come to warm themselves
short: Christ burns for humanity, yet no one comes to his fire: 'He came unto his own, and his own received him not' (John 1:11).
body: The lament that no one approaches to warm their hearts at his fire recalls John 1:11 and the image, at the Nativity, of the inn with no room. The disciples on the road to Emmaus later say 'Did not our heart burn within us?' (Luke 24:32). In Southwell's England, where Catholic worship was illegal, the reproach could also be heard as addressed to a nation that had turned away from the old faith. The speaker himself, warmed at the start, is the exception.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), John 1:11
The Bible (KJV), Luke 24:32

anchor: My faultless breast the furnace is
title: The furnace conceit
short: An allegory of a refiner's furnace: breast the furnace, thorns the fuel, love the fire, sighs the smoke, shames the ashes.
body: The child's speech develops a sustained allegory, a conceit of the kind later associated with the metaphysical poets. His sinless ('faultless') breast is the furnace, the fuel is 'wounding thorns' (the crown of thorns), love is the fire, sighs the smoke, and the 'shames and scorns' of the Passion are the ashes. The furnace recalls the refiner's fire of Malachi 3:2-3 and 'the furnace of affliction' (Isaiah 48:10). Each element is carefully assigned, in a manner like an emblem with its explanation.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Malachi 3:2-3
The Bible (KJV), Isaiah 48:10
James H. McDonald and Nancy Pollard Brown (eds), The Poems of Robert Southwell, S.J. (Oxford, 1967)

title: The thorns
short: The crown of thorns (Matthew 27:29): the Passion is already present at Christmas.
body: The 'wounding thorns' are the crown of thorns placed on Christ's head before the crucifixion (Matthew 27:29; John 19:2). Making them the fuel of the furnace means that Christ's suffering nourishes the fire of his love. The anticipation of the Passion in the Nativity was common in devotional art and poetry, where the infant is shown with emblems of the cross.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Matthew 27:29
James H. McDonald and Nancy Pollard Brown (eds), The Poems of Robert Southwell, S.J. (Oxford, 1967)

title: Love the fire
short: Love is the fire of the furnace: the language of the Petrarchan lover's sighs, transferred to Christ.
body: The line reuses the commonplace of the love lyric, the lover's burning heart and smoking sighs, and gives it to Christ, whose love for humanity is the true fire. Compare Romeo's 'Love is a smoke made with the fume of sighs' (Romeo and Juliet 1.1). Southwell's project of rescuing poetry from profane love for divine subjects is visible here. The smoke of sighs is the visible sign of the invisible fire.

sources.cite: William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet, 1.1 (Folger Shakespeare)
James H. McDonald and Nancy Pollard Brown (eds), The Poems of Robert Southwell, S.J. (Oxford, 1967)

title: Justice and Mercy
short: Justice feeds the fire and Mercy blows the coals: the 'Four Daughters of God' (Psalm 85:10) reconciled in Christ.
body: Justice lays on the fuel (the demands of divine justice that require sacrifice) while Mercy blows the coals (fans the fire of love). The pairing recalls the medieval allegory of the Four Daughters of God, Mercy, Truth, Justice and Peace, based on Psalm 85:10 ('Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other'), in which the virtues debate humanity's fate and are reconciled by the Incarnation. Here both work together in the same furnace.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Psalm 85:10
James H. McDonald and Nancy Pollard Brown (eds), The Poems of Robert Southwell, S.J. (Oxford, 1967)

anchor: The metal in this furnace wrought
title: The metal refined
short: Human souls are the metal: defiled by sin, they are worked and refined in the furnace of Christ's love.
body: The furnace is now a smelter or forge, and the 'metal ... wrought' (worked, refined) is 'men's defiled souls'. The image draws on Malachi 3:3, where God 'shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver', purifying his people. Christ's suffering is the means of their purification: he burns 'To work them to their good'. The process of refining by fire was a familiar image of spiritual purification in devotional writing.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Malachi 3:3
James H. McDonald and Nancy Pollard Brown (eds), The Poems of Robert Southwell, S.J. (Oxford, 1967)

title: The bath of blood
short: The fire will melt into a bath of blood to wash souls: Revelation 1:5 and 7:14, and the sacraments.
body: The final metamorphosis: fire becomes liquid, a bath in which the child will 'wash them in my blood'. The idea derives from Revelation 1:5 ('washed us from our sins in his own blood') and 7:14 ('washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb'). Readers often hear an allusion to baptism and the Eucharist, the sacraments by which Catholics believed Christ's blood was applied to the soul. The logic of the poem moves from fire to water to blood.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Revelation 1:5
The Bible (KJV), Revelation 7:14
James H. McDonald and Nancy Pollard Brown (eds), The Poems of Robert Southwell, S.J. (Oxford, 1967)

title: Christmas Day
short: The vision vanishes and the speaker remembers the date: the meaning of the Nativity is the Passion.
body: The vision 'vanish'd out of sight / And swiftly shrunk away', and the speaker 'straight' (immediately) recalls 'That it was Christmas Day'. The ending is a quiet recognition that turns the poem into a meditation on the feast: the newborn child is already the suffering Saviour, and Christmas means sacrifice. The plain last line can be read as anticlimax or, more often, as deliberate understatement. The poem sits beside Southwell's companion Nativity poems such as 'New Prince, New Pomp'.
